summary: Defines a MIB for monitoring the performance of Service Level Agreements that are set up through policy definitions. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: If a service promises to be fast, this provides a way to measure whether it kept that promise.

questions: how to monitor service level agreements with snmp
how to track network sla performance
subtitle: An SNMP-based MIB for tracking Service Level Agreement performance metrics.

tldr.problem: Organizations need to track whether their network services are meeting promised performance levels, such as delivery speed and reliability, but lacked a standard way to collect and report these Service Level Agreement metrics.
tldr.mechanism: SLAPM-MIB defines a set of SNMP Management Information Base objects that collect statistics on policy-based traffic rules, allowing network managers to monitor rates, delays, and connection data across policy-controlled flows.
tldr.outcome: The RFC remained experimental and has not achieved widespread deployment as a standard, but provided a framework for SNMP-based SLA monitoring that could be adapted by vendors.

facts.label: Main tables
facts.value: 5 (including policy names, stats, monitoring, and subcomponents)

today: RFC 2758 is an Experimental protocol and has not been advanced to Standards Track. It has remained in limited use, with vendors and operators occasionally implementing aspects of the framework for proprietary SLA monitoring systems. The core concepts of policy-based monitoring influenced later network management approaches, though the specific SLAPM-MIB structure has not achieved wide deployment.

sections.title: What SLAs Are and Why They Matter
sections.content:
A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is a promise that a network service will perform at a certain level—for example, delivering data at minimum speeds or keeping delays below a threshold. Network managers need to know whether their systems are keeping these promises.

RFC 2758 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for SNMP, the standard protocol for collecting network management data. The SLAPM-MIB (Service Level Agreement Performance Monitoring MIB) provides a way to gather and report statistics about how well policy-based network traffic rules are performing.
sections.plainLanguage: Just like a school tracks test scores to see if students are learning, a network tracks SLA metrics to see if it is delivering on its promises.

sections.title: The MIB Structure
sections.content:
The SLAPM-MIB has five main parts: scalar objects for global settings, the slapmPolicyNameTable that maps numeric index values to policy rule names, the slapmPolicyRuleStatsTable that holds per-policy statistics, the slapmPRMonTable that sets up monitoring thresholds, and the slapmSubcomponentTable that tracks individual connections or listeners.

The design evolved over time to use numeric indexes instead of policy names directly, because policy definitions became too complex to use as MIB table indexes. A separate name table now provides the mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is organized like file folders: one folder holds the names of policies, another holds statistics for each policy, another holds monitoring rules, and another tracks individual conversations.

sections.title: What Gets Monitored
sections.content:
The MIB allows monitoring of minimum and maximum data transfer rates (in kilobits per second) and maximum delay (in milliseconds). When the current rate or delay crosses a threshold, the MIB can trigger a notification to alert managers.

For individual connections, the subcomponent table tracks octets sent and received, round-trip times for TCP connections, the number of protocol data units (segments or datagrams), and the associated application name if known. The RFC supports both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB watches three things: Is data moving fast enough? Is it moving too fast? And are packets arriving without too much delay? When something goes wrong, it sends a warning.

sections.title: Policy Administration and Data Collection
sections.content:
Policy definitions themselves are managed outside the scope of this MIB; the RFC assumes an external policy framework defines which traffic rules apply. The SLAPM-MIB reflects the current set of active policy rules as table entries, and agents automatically populate these entries as policies are defined or removed.

The slapmPRMonTable is the only table that supports row creation and deletion via SNMP, allowing management applications to set up monitoring sessions. An owner index in this table enables access control under SNMP's VACM security model.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB listens to an outside system that creates the actual traffic rules, then automatically creates report entries for each one. Only the monitoring table lets managers add or remove monitoring sessions through SNMP.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The MIB contains information that may be sensitive—for example, traffic patterns and performance metrics could reveal network capacity and usage. Authentication of SNMP requests and controlled access are recommended. The RFC leaves the details to the SNMP Administrative Framework.

The slapmPRMonTable and slapmSubcomponentTable should not be deployed in insecure environments. The owner-index design allows a security administrator to use SNMP's View-Based Access Control Model (VACM) to grant each user or group access only to monitoring entries they created.
sections.plainLanguage: This information is like security camera footage—you probably don't want everyone seeing it. The MIB uses SNMP security features to keep that information private.
